cross_module_architecture.dimension_character: The compile-time architecture is genuinely strong: an acyclic, layered crate graph with a deliberate zero-dependency contract hub (agent-protocol) and services that coordinate through typed NATS envelopes rather than import edges. The weakness is concentrated at the runtime boundary those crates share: the message-contract layer is fragmented (five copies of the activity event, three copies of InvokeResponse, one off-contract publisher), the central router has an unbounded republish loop for non-Envelope traffic, and the intended shared agent runtime in agent-core sits unused while binaries hand-roll parallel machinery. A new team member learns the crate map in 30 seconds; the bus behavior holds several surprises the docs actively misdescribe.
cross_module_architecture.score_rationale: Between the 80 anchor (solid but uneven, recurring boundary friction) and 70 (mixed, patterns not fully trustworthy). The dependency direction, hub design, and facade discipline push toward 90; the DLQ self-loop on `ares.*`, the drifted activity contract, the bypassed HttpToolGateway resilience contract, and the dead checkpoint path pull toward 70. The defects are real and systemic but confined to one seam (the NATS boundary), so 74.0.

high_level_elegance.dimension_character: The crate-level decomposition is genuinely legible: every top-level package names a security-operations capability, protocol types are separated from transport, and a newcomer can sketch the 21-crate map in minutes. The blur sits one layer up, in ownership claims that the runtime does not honour — README's 'tool-server is the only path to side effects', agent-core's advertised agent runtime that nothing instantiates, one kill switch implemented twice with different semantics, and a service/agent inventory that has already fallen two subsystems behind (ACP, vuln-agent). A developer therefore learns the structure quickly but learns the *responsibilities* wrongly, and pays for it the first time they touch a write path, the safety control, or the agent roster.
high_level_elegance.score_rationale: The decomposition, naming and pattern consistency alone sit near the 90 anchor (clear ownership, only minor boundary blur). It is pulled down to the high 70s because four of the first questions a new engineer asks have wrong or missing answers in code: who owns writes (duplicated between connectors and gated tools), where the agent runtime lives (a dead crate), which kill-switch semantics apply (two implementations), and which services exist (docs list 9 of 10, README 11 of 21 crates). The defects are structural but concentrated in contract ownership rather than in the crate graph, so 78.0.

convention_outlier.dimension_character: The infrastructure half of the workspace (agent-protocol, agent-core, api-server, tool-server, connectors, policy-engine, cvss) is genuinely uniform — one executor protocol, one accessor vocabulary, one error strategy per layer, one test placement — so a developer who learns api-server or executors can predict the next module they open. The drift is concentrated in the five agent binaries and in the Cargo manifests: four agents copy-paste the same `activity.rs` while the fifth hand-rolls a different payload shape, the kill-switch protocol is applied by three agents and skipped by two, and the manifests split 7/14 on declaration style with no role-based rationale. The result is a codebase where the shared libraries are trustworthy but the agent family and build files require reading each sibling individually.
convention_outlier.score_rationale: The score sits at the 80 anchor ('noticeable convention drift across major areas') rather than above it: the agent crates are the product's core subsystem and they diverge on the activity contract, subject-constant ownership, kill-switch protocol and boot skeleton, and 14 of 21 manifests contradict the other 7. It is held above 70 by how disciplined the rest is — no naming drift at all across 21 crates, one plugin protocol for ~20 executors, and error/test/doc conventions that split cleanly by layer — so the friction is localised and mechanical rather than pervasive.

error_consistency.dimension_character: Error handling here is designed rather than accidental: library crates expose typed thiserror enums, binaries propagate anyhow with .context(), every agent wraps its message loop in the same log-and-continue boundary, and the policy engine expresses failure as a Deny verdict instead of an error. The friction is concentrated at seams where the same job is implemented more than once — the kill switch, the /invoke client, the HTTP error envelope, and intel parsing — where sibling code paths disagree about whether a failure is an error, a null, or a log line. A developer can predict propagation inside any single crate, but not always across two crates doing the same thing.
error_consistency.score_rationale: The core propagation story is strong and uniform (Result everywhere, typed errors at library boundaries, documented resilience table, fail-closed idempotency, no production panics), which places this well above the 80 'mixed strategies' anchor. It stops short of the 90 'occasional inconsistencies that don't cause real confusion' anchor because several inconsistencies do cause real confusion: a transport failure is reported as a policy Deny (crates/response-agent/src/main.rs:210-232), a missing credential is reported as success (crates/tool-server/src/executors/mod.rs:35-37), a Postgres error is reported as a detection miss (crates/bas-runner/src/main.rs:130-167), and the kill switch is documented fail-closed but implemented fail-open (docs/services.md:32 vs crates/agent-core/src/kill.rs:28-33).

naming_quality.dimension_character: Naming is a genuine strength of this codebase: protocol types, pipeline stages, state machines and predicates are named for the role they play, and nearly every module opens with a doc header that fixes its vocabulary before the code uses it. The defects are localized and shallow — a few generic verbs sitting exactly where a newcomer enters (the per-envelope handler, the tool dispatch path), one opaque `St`, and a couple of variant/polarity choices that read against the neighbouring names. Nothing systemic: the same developer who trips on `execute`/`run_tool` in tool-server will read `draft_sigma`/`promote_and_commit` and know the pipeline order without opening the file.
naming_quality.score_rationale: The codebase sits at the 90 anchor — names are mostly precise and a handful require a second look — with the second look concentrated in tool-server's execute/run_tool inversion and the two `process` handlers, which is why it lands slightly below. It is clearly above the 80 anchor: I found no case of routine ambiguity, and generic verbs (process, execute, handle) appear in single digits across 13.7k LOC. The positives are structural rather than cosmetic — vocabulary is defined per module and held consistently across five agent binaries, so the isolated defects do not undermine the pattern.

abstraction_fitness.dimension_character: The load-bearing abstractions are excellent and boring in the right way: agent-protocol is the single shared contract, the Tool trait carries 20+ executors behind one registry, the idempotency store shares a pure state machine across two backends, and the rate limiter takes policy as a fn pointer. The failures are all of one kind — abstractions that exist but are not wired: agent-core's entire agent loop, gateway and checkpointer have no production caller, ModelRouter routes between two identical providers, and the activity-event contract was copied per service instead of living in agent-protocol. A developer would trust the protocol/policy/tool layer immediately and then repeatedly discover that the orchestration layer they were told to use is bypassed by every binary.
abstraction_fitness.score_rationale: Strong, honest seams in the contract and tool layers pull the score up, and most code is direct rather than layered (no pass-through chains, only one pure forwarder, five traits of which four have two real impls). It lands in the 70s because the friction is systemic rather than isolated: an unused control-loop crate, four-to-five copies of one wire type, getters that silently construct clients, a rollback map pointing at tools that policy forbids, and a policy context field nothing populates — each one a 'why is this different / why does this exist?' moment for the next developer.

dependency_health.dimension_character: The dependency set is small, acyclic and mostly purposeful: one runtime, one HTTP client, one JSON/date/hash library each, workspace-inherited versions, and a thin dev-dependency surface. The drift that does exist is concentrated and very visible - reqwest links both OpenSSL and rustls, an archived YAML parser sits on every config path, nine declared dependencies are never referenced, and a dead pgvector entry coexists with two crates that bypass workspace inheritance for a reason their comments no longer support. A developer would trust the shape of the set but hit recurring 'why is this declared?' and 'why is this compiled twice?' moments.
dependency_health.score_rationale: The rubric's 80 anchor is exactly 'duplicate libraries for the same purpose, heavy deps for light use, or other signs the dependency set has drifted', and this codebase shows both textbook symptoms (dual TLS backends from an un-disabled default feature; tokio 'full' inherited by crates that need two modules) plus an unmaintained parser on the config path and nine unused declarations. What keeps it above 60 is the underlying discipline: single library per concern, one workspace spec per dependency, a lockfile that resolves offline, and no cycles or conflicting pins inside the workspace. The friction is real but each item is a small, local edit rather than a structural blocker.

low_level_elegance.dimension_character: Inside any single function this codebase is disciplined and easy to read: guard clauses instead of nesting, named constants with the reason in a comment, exhaustive matches over closed enums, one pure transition function where state machines are involved, and a control loop that has no boolean flags. The friction is almost entirely horizontal rather than vertical — moving between two sibling functions or two sibling crates, a developer meets the same small job written twice with slightly different shapes (a helper used by one method and inlined by its twin, two identical 21-line encoders, an identical rate-limit builder, five hex encoders), plus a few statements that survive a refactor and no longer do anything.
low_level_elegance.score_rationale: This sits at the 80 anchor rather than 90 because the unevenness is recurring and occasionally consequential, not isolated: the rate-limit classifier enumerates A2A and forgets the sibling ACP routes (crates/api-server/src/ratelimit.rs:29-50), the severity-to-integer mapping exists twice with different defaults (crates/triage-agent/src/main.rs:173-178 vs crates/vuln-agent/src/main.rs:86-94), and `cancel_run` carries a branch whose two arms are the same code (crates/api-server/src/acp.rs:459-483). It stays well clear of 70 because no function requires untangling to follow, nesting never exceeds three levels in production paths, and the defensive/ceremonial sprawl the rubric warns about is absent — the defects are copy-paste and leftovers, each fixable by deleting or pointing one call site at an existing helper.

mid_level_elegance.dimension_character: The shared vocabulary is genuinely shared - envelope, tool call, decision and handoff types all live in agent-protocol and every service speaks them - but the adapters around that vocabulary are rebuilt per service, so the same three handoffs (invoke a tool, publish an envelope, report activity) exist in three to six variants with subtly different semantics. A new team member can read the message types in 30 seconds and still be wrong about how a message actually crosses a boundary, because the real contracts are conventions (HTTP 200 carries a deny, the retryable flag hides in result.output, the case id lives inside a thehive:// URI, activity events may omit workflow_run_id) that live in whichever caller happens to implement them. The library-shaped abstractions in agent-core (ToolGateway, CheckpointStore, AgentLoop) are well composed but bypassed by the binaries, which is the clearest symptom of the seam problem rather than a separate one.
mid_level_elegance.score_rationale: Upward: the protocol crate is disciplined and single-sourced, several seams are documented at the point of definition, the idempotency and retry contracts are explicit and fail-closed, and ACP demonstrably reuses the A2A dispatch path instead of copying it. Downward: the recurring pattern is that each new service re-derives the transport seam, which has already produced a policy denial being logged as success (detection-agent), a transport error being recorded as a policy denial (response-agent), an unenforced protected-asset rule, and an orchestrator DLQ that feeds itself; that is more than isolated friction and sits below the 80 anchor, where a developer 'mostly' trusts patterns seen elsewhere. The score lands at 70 - mixed: individual seams are small and well commented, but a cross-module change still requires knowing which of several variants the caller in front of you chose.

test_strategy.dimension_character: Test craft is genuinely strong where it exists — deterministic clock injection, stub backends behind traits, security-focused assertions on the shell allowlist and idempotency state machine, and reference-vector CVSS checks — and the suite is green with no snapshot overuse or timing races. But the portfolio is concentrated in library crates: every service binary, all of the api-server HTTP surface, the connectors HTTP layer, the detection pipeline, and the tool-server policy->audit->idempotency->execute composition have zero direct tests, and there is no integration-test surface at all. A developer would trust the units they can see and be blind exactly where autonomy and side effects live.
test_strategy.score_rationale: The dimension sits below the 70 'mixed' anchor and near 60 'significant drag': 68 tests over ~13.9k LOC with 44 of 63 files untested means meaningful risk is unvalidated in the paths that matter most (tool invocation, agent verdict/plan routing, alert dedupe, webhook ingestion). What pulls it above 60 is the reliability and intent of the tests that do exist — explicit assertions, injectable time, trait-based stubs, and a real policy-gate suite that encodes the deny-by-default contract — plus a documented 19-row policy matrix and a golden-set directory that show the strategy is understood even where it is unfinished.

api_surface_coherence.dimension_character: The protocol and library layers are unusually coherent for a workspace this young: ACP and A2A each have one typed error model, one dispatcher, and enums for every state machine, and the connector clients share a single constructor and retry contract. The incoherence sits exactly where services talk to each other: three different HTTP error-body shapes in one axum app, three independent copies of the `/invoke` wire contract interpreted three different ways, and a tool-argument contract that is defined once in policy YAML and again (with different names) in executor code. A developer can predict a crate's API from reading one sibling, but cannot predict a service's HTTP or tool-call behavior from one example.
api_surface_coherence.score_rationale: Strong single-purpose crates (acp, a2a, llm-client, http-limits, cvss) and consistent trait boundaries pull the score up toward the 80 anchor. What pulls it down is recurring, load-bearing irregularity on the platform's busiest boundary: a documented `{error: string}` contract that most endpoints ignore, `/invoke` clients that disagree on what the response means (one fabricates a policy denial from a transport error, one ignores the verdict entirely), and no discoverable tool schema. That is the '80 = solid but uneven' band shading toward 70, so the score lands in the mid-70s.

authorization_consistency.dimension_character: One authorization layer is genuinely well built — a centralized, deny-by-default PolicyEngine with a fixed check order, compiled arg schemas, a protected-asset boundary and hash-chained audit of every verdict — but it guards only the tool-call path. Everything around it is inconsistent: none of the three HTTP services authenticates a caller, the global kill switch is unauthenticated, unaudited and not wired to the enforcement point, approval identity is a self-asserted string defaulting to 'operator', and triage/hunt/detection/bas-runner reach the same external effects (TheHive cases, OpenSearch monitors, git commits, ssh commands) without passing through the gate. A security reviewer would find the tool boundary trustworthy and the rest of the trust model unverifiable.
authorization_consistency.score_rationale: The score sits at the 60 anchor ('auth posture is inconsistent; a developer reviewing security cannot trust that coverage is complete') because coverage is genuinely mixed rather than uniformly absent: the same TheHive case creation is both an allowlisted audited tool and a direct unpoliced client call, and the kill switch advertises control it does not exercise. What pulls it up from the 40s is real substance in the one gate that exists — deny-by-default policy, defense-in-depth executor validation, per-decision audit chaining, and gaps honestly catalogued in docs/services.md with scripts/api-security-check.sh. What keeps it out of the 70s and 80s is that nothing verifies who is calling, so none of the good patterns can be attributed to a principal or enforced per-object.

ai_generated_debt.dimension_character: The codebase reads as purpose-driven where it matters: security-critical modules (policy-engine, idempotency, approvals, connectors) carry WHY comments, deliberate degraded-mode helpers, and no entry/exit logging. Around that core, generation-shaped ceremony accumulates in the seams: five agent binaries each carry their own ActivityEvent/emit/main scaffold, an entire unused agent-core framework sits waiting for a caller, and every public item is fronted by a doc line that restates its own name. A newcomer would follow the triage or tool-server flow in 30 seconds, then lose that confidence when they hit agent-core or the vuln-agent activity shape and cannot tell which of the parallel implementations is live.
ai_generated_debt.score_rationale: Strong anchors push up: comments explain constraints rather than narrate code, defensive checks cluster at real trust boundaries (env, HTTP, Postgres), and duplicated retry/backoff logic is at least bounded and documented. What pulls the score below the 'solid but uneven' line is volume of formulaic duplication — 5 activity-event copies (one already drifted), 4 hex encoders, 2 base64url encoders, 2 JetStream bootstraps, 2 SSE state machines, 2 kill-switch implementations with different semantics — plus ~545 LOC of never-instantiated framework in agent-core that makes real read paths unreachable. These are small individually but recur across crates, so a developer meets 'why is this different here?' repeatedly.

incomplete_migration.dimension_character: The small migrations were finished properly and their old paths deleted — axum 0.8 routes, one NVD 2.0 client, one shared rate limiter, no deprecated symbols anywhere — so a developer never trips over half-renamed helpers or compatibility aliases. The exceptions are structural and sit exactly where new code is most likely to land: agent-core ships a complete agent runtime that no service instantiates, so every agent keeps its own loop and its own /invoke client with different failure semantics, and the connectors layer is narrow enough that three callers still reach OpenSearch and TheHive with hand-rolled reqwest. Around those two seams sit genuine leftovers (dead `os` field, unused pgvector dependency, `API_BIND` in the manifests, docs still claiming no rate limiting), which reinforce the impression that the last wave of consolidation stopped mid-way.
incomplete_migration.score_rationale: The anchors place 80 at 'old and new patterns coexisting — unclear which to follow or extend', and that is literally the state of the agent runtime and the outbound HTTP layer, the two places a developer extends most often; the divergent retry/deny behaviour between the three /invoke clients makes the ambiguity operational, not cosmetic. What keeps this above the 70 mark is that the rest of the codebase demonstrates completed migrations with the old path removed and enforced by tests (route-syntax guard, single NVD client, shared limiter, ACP reusing A2A), plus the complete absence of deprecated-but-called symbols. The residue items are cheap and well-bounded; the two dual-path seams are what hold the score in the mid-70s.

package_organization.dimension_character: The crate-level map is genuinely navigable: 21 focused members with documented ownership in README and docs/services.md, a private-module/facade pattern in agent-core, and several small service crates split cleanly by responsibility. The weakness is one level down and at the seams: four flat modules absorb a quarter of the codebase (connectors, executors/mod, policy-engine, enrichment-lib), and concerns that cross crate boundaries — the activity wire contract, the kill switch, the policies directory — have no owning module, so they were copied and have already diverged. A developer can predict which crate to open, but inside several crates and along the operator-control seam they must read the implementation to know where the truth lives.
package_organization.score_rationale: Against the anchors this is 'solid but uneven': the strengths are systemic (documented ownership, consistent per-service layout, shared http-limits/agent-protocol crates with 13 and 9 importers) and the defects are concentrated in a handful of files and seams, which is why the score sits in the high 70s rather than lower. What pulls it down is measurable: 27% of LOC in single modules with no submodule boundary, a duplicated activity contract that already emits a non-conforming event from vuln-agent, a kill switch whose two implementations disagree on a whitespace-only kill file, and module names that shadow the crates they call. Fixing the four monoliths and giving operator-control plumbing one home would move this dimension into the 90s without touching the crate graph.

initialization_coupling.dimension_character: Structurally this is a clean Rust workspace: there is no mutable module-scope state at all, the only statics are two lazily initialized pure values, and every service builds its state in `main` and injects it as `Arc<AppState>`/`Arc<Deps>`, so a developer can import any crate without worrying about import-time side effects or boot ordering. The fragility sits one layer up, at the seam between boot and runtime: configuration is resolved in two competing planes (boot-time `ConnectorConfig` versus per-call `env::var` with different empty-string semantics), the safety-critical kill switch has two implementations that disagree on edge cases, and table/schema ownership is documented per crate but implemented inside service binaries - including an `audit_log` table that nothing ever creates.
initialization_coupling.score_rationale: The absence of global singletons and the uniform explicit-initialization pattern push this well above the 60 'boot behavior is routinely fragile' anchor and above a naive reading of the per-call env reads. It lands in the mixed 70s because the remaining defects are reproducible and not merely stylistic: an exported `ARES_KILL_SWITCH=1` flips the policy-engine test suite, a whitespace-only `policies/kill` engages the agents but not the tool server, api-server's TheHive helper sends an empty bearer token that the connector path would never send, and `audit_log` - read by api-server and bas-runner, written by tool-server - has no initializer anywhere in the repo, so tool decisions fail to audit at runtime.

design_coherence.dimension_character: Locally the design is disciplined: policy evaluation is a documented nine-step ladder, the idempotency protocol is a single pure transition shared by two stores, and the detection pipeline is one function per stage. At the seams it drifts: an entire control-loop layer in agent-core is built and never wired while four agents each hand-roll the same scaffolding, and the two protocol surfaces (A2A and ACP) duplicate the same persistence fold and SSE state machine. A new team member would read any single file quickly but would not be able to answer 'where does the agent framework live?' in 30 seconds, and the kill switch has two implementations that can disagree about whether the platform is halted.
design_coherence.score_rationale: Well above the 'significant drag' anchor because every module has a stated responsibility, deliberate shortcuts are labelled where they occur, and repeated shapes usually share a pure core rather than copy logic. Held at the 'mixed' band by three structural facts that recur across crates: an unused abstraction layer with a dead data path behind it, agent-level scaffolding copied four to five times, and duplicated protocol machinery in the crate that already owns both protocols.

contract_coherence.dimension_character: Contract hygiene is the codebase's strongest habit at the type level — traits, wire types and documented invariants match their implementations almost everywhere, and modules routinely document their own limits and known gaps instead of pretending completeness. The friction is at the seams: contracts stated in one crate are broken by a sibling (rollback tools that policy forbids, `sync` mode that returns before terminal, `Ok(None)` for a 404), and a handful of docstrings promise clamping, aborting or reporting that the code does not perform. A developer can trust the shapes and most behaviors, but must verify the aspirational half of the documentation.
contract_coherence.score_rationale: This sits at solid-but-uneven (80): the shared contract crates (agent-protocol, a2a, acp, http-limits, idempotency) are exemplary, and honest 'known gap' docs are a real strength, which pushes the score up. It is held below 90 by ten recurring divergences — a task marked `completed` on a kill-switch step, `Status::Approved` for calls that never executed, a documented 404-to-`None` mapping that returns `Err`, and a rollback path the allowlist makes unreachable — each a case where a developer reading the contract would be wrong.

logic_clarity.dimension_character: Control flow is mostly direct and deliberate: the security-critical paths (policy evaluation, idempotency claims, tool dispatch) are written as flat guard-clause pipelines with numbered or tabulated ordering, so a reader can trace a decision without surprises. The defects are small and scattered rather than systemic — an unreachable retry branch, a duplicate return block, two no-op statements, an async API that never awaits — but two of them break the 'provably does what it claims' promise outright: rollback entries name tools that exist nowhere in the allowlist, and dry-run BAS mode still writes results and triggers detection. A developer would trust the hot paths and be tripped up only at these seams.
logic_clarity.score_rationale: The score sits in the solid-but-uneven band because the dominant impression is of purposeful, well-commented control flow (a pure idempotency state machine, documented check order, fail-closed error paths), which pushes it above 80, while roughly one dead or contradictory construct per service pulls it back down. The 85+ anchors require that a developer hit only isolated simplification opportunities; here the dead branches and the documented-but-unimplemented compensation path are more than isolated, and the fail-open severity filter is a latent correctness trap. Hence 82.5 rather than the high 80s.

type_safety.dimension_character: Structural typing is genuinely strong: protocol states, message payloads and error kinds are enums with explicit wire conversions, public APIs are documented, and production code almost never short-circuits a typed Option. The weakness is domain vocabulary — severity, verdict, decision, IoC type, provider name and agent step are bare strings re-declared in each crate, matched with `_ =>` fallbacks that fail open, and two return types (`Tool::execute`, `invoke_tool`) cannot express what actually happened. A developer trusts the shapes and the protocol enums immediately, but must read each call site to learn which spelling of a severity or decision it expects.
type_safety.score_rationale: Against the anchors this sits just below 'solid but uneven': the enum discipline in a2a/acp/agent-protocol and the absence of production unwraps would justify 85+, but the repeated string vocabularies and lossy fallbacks (severity rank 0 on a typo, unknown task state read as Submitted, transport error recorded as a policy deny) are recurring friction a developer would hit across modules rather than isolated soft spots. It is well above 60 — annotations are not unreliable and the runtime can be predicted from the types in almost every case — so 78.0 reflects strong structural typing dragged down by untyped domain vocabulary.

issues.summary: Orchestrator's `ares.*` subscription DLQ-loops every non-Envelope message forever
issues.suggestion: In handle_message, return early when `msg.subject` is SUBJECT_DLQ or is not one of the routed ingress subjects (or subscribe only to `ares.alerts` plus explicit command subjects); before any DLQ republish, write an `ares-dlq-count` header and drop when it exceeds MAX_DELIVERIES — that makes the documented 3-delivery contract real and kills the loop.
evidence: orchestrator/main.rs:139 subscribes `ares.*`, which matches ares.dlq, ares.activity and ares.vulns; main.rs:69-75 republishes every unparseable payload to SUBJECT_DLQ unconditionally — a message received ON ares.dlq that fails Envelope parsing is republished to ares.dlq and re-received, with no exit condition

Non-Envelope traffic is routine: ActivityEvent JSON from four agents and vuln advisories both fail `serde_json::from_slice::<Envelope>` (missing id/correlation_id/source/kind/payload), so every routine activity event enters an infinite DLQ republish cycle — unbounded bus amplification at the central router

delivery_count (main.rs:120-127) reads a `Nats-Delivery-Count` header nothing ever sets on core-NATS publishes, so MAX_DELIVERIES=3 can never trip; the documented 'drop only on ares.dlq after 3 deliveries' contract (docs/services.md:48) is inert
Self-republish of routed envelopes is guarded (main.rs:90 `msg.subject.as_str() == subject`) but no equivalent guard exists for ares.dlq or for non-Envelope subjects

evidence: Four near-identical activity.rs files define ActivityEvent + `SUBJECT_ACTIVITY = "ares.activity"`; api-server/stream.rs:22 defines a fifth copy of the constant; vuln-agent/main.rs:29 defines a sixth

Drift already happened: triage's copy uses `step: &'static str` vs `String` elsewhere, and vuln-agent emits a hand-built json! event (main.rs:121-126) lacking `workflow_run_id` — a required field of the documented SSE schema `{workflow_run_id, agent, step, detail, ts}` (docs/services.md:33) and the correlation join api-server performs (acp.rs:201, a2a.rs)

issues.suggestion: Either drop the publish (the table is the real delivery channel today) or make it contractual: move SUBJECT_VULNS into agent-protocol and publish an Envelope with a suitable kind so the message participates in routing instead of the DLQ.
evidence: main.rs:27 defines `SUBJECT_VULNS` locally and main.rs:236-249 publishes a bare json! advisory — no Envelope wrapper, breaking the platform convention that 'every service speaks the types defined' in agent-protocol (agent-protocol/lib.rs:3-4)

issues.suggestion: Move `b64url` and a hex encoder into one leaf crate both callers already depend on (connectors for b64url, agent-protocol for hex), and turn the duplicated `ratelimit::build` into `http_limits::build(classify: fn(&Request) -> Tier)` so api-server and ingestion-gateway pass only their classifier.

`pub fn build() -> Arc<RateLimiter>` is byte-identical in crates/api-server/src/ratelimit.rs:11-17 and crates/ingestion-gateway/src/ratelimit.rs:11-17, including the POLICIES_DIR resolution and the spawn_idle_purge call.

Lowercase-hex encoding is written five times: crates/audit/src/lib.rs:141-145 (`sha256_hex`), crates/orchestrator/src/dedupe.rs:83-86 (a whole `mod hex` justified as 'to avoid an extra dependency'), crates/tool-server/src/idempotency.rs:117-121, crates/response-agent/src/main.rs:367-369 (`fn hex`), and inline in enrichment-lib's Sha256 formatting.

issues.summary: ProviderLookup has five match arms that each repeat the same send → error_for_status → json chain
issues.suggestion: Add one private helper in executors/mod.rs (e.g. `async fn send_json(req: RequestBuilder, label: &str) -> Result<Value>`) and reduce each arm to `send_json(http().get(url).header(...), "virustotal").await`; the per-provider `.context()` strings can move into the label argument.
evidence: crates/tool-server/src/executors/mod.rs:407-493: the virustotal, abuseipdb, shodan, greynoise and urlscan arms each build a request and then repeat the identical 8-line tail `.send().await.context("<provider> request")?.error_for_status().context("<provider> HTTP error")?.json::<Value>().await?`.
Only the request construction differs between arms (URL, header name, query vs json body), so the arm bodies are ~20 lines each where ~6 would do.

The same shape already exists as a helper elsewhere — `json_ok` in crates/connectors/src/lib.rs:50-53 does error_for_status + json decode — but it is private to that crate, so tool-server re-derives it five times (plus once more in SlackNotify at 554-564 and EntraUser at 524-533).
A reader has to compare five arms line by line to confirm the error semantics really are identical, which is exactly the cost the duplication imposes.

issues.summary: classify() enumerates A2A paths for the expensive/stream tiers but omits the parallel ACP routes it was cloned for
issues.suggestion: Extend classify() with the ACP siblings: treat `POST /acp/runs` (and `/acp/runs/{id}` resume/cancel) as Tier::Expensive and `GET /acp/runs/{id}/events` as Tier::Stream, matching the existing `/a2a/` branches, and add the two cases to the `classify_maps_paths_to_tiers` test at crates/api-server/src/ratelimit.rs:68-104.
evidence: crates/api-server/src/ratelimit.rs:29-50 returns Tier::Stream only for `/stream/activity` and `/a2a/tasks/*/events`, and Tier::Expensive only for `/cvss/score` and paths starting with `/a2a/`.

crates/api-server/src/main.rs:311-321 registers the ACP surface in the same router: `POST /acp/runs` (which dispatches an agent run) falls through to Tier::General (60/s burst 120), and `GET /acp/runs/{run_id}/events` is an SSE stream that is request-counted instead of concurrency-capped.
So the same operation costs a different bucket depending on which protocol front-end the client speaks, and a long-lived ACP stream burns tokens until the client disconnects.

issues.summary: The severity → TheHive integer mapping is written twice with different defaults (2 vs 0) for the same unknown input
issues.suggestion: Put a single `fn case_severity(sev: &str) -> u8` next to `NewCase` in the connectors crate (low=1, medium=2, high=3, critical=4, unknown=2) and have both agents call it; keep vuln-agent's `severity_rank` only for the `>= min_rank` comparison.
evidence: crates/triage-agent/src/main.rs:173-178 maps low=1, high=3, critical=4 and everything else (including medium and any unrecognized string) to 2.

crates/vuln-agent/src/main.rs:86-94 defines `severity_rank` mapping low=1..critical=4 with `_ => 0`, and line 258 reuses that comparison rank as the case's `severity` field (`severity: severity_rank(&severity)`), so an unrecognized severity produces a TheHive case with severity 0 instead of the triage agent's 2.

The two functions also disagree on ordering semantics: triage's version is a presentation mapping that skips 2 for 'medium' by falling into `_`, vuln's is a comparison rank — one function is doing two jobs.

issues.summary: A no-op `drop(ctx.counters.get(&ck))` in the blast-radius branch implies a lock release that does not exist
issues.suggestion: Delete line 416. If the intent was to make the guard's lifetime explicit, keep the `if let` block scoped (it already is) rather than adding a second `get`.
evidence: crates/policy-engine/src/lib.rs:408-417: the cooldown read is scoped inside `if let Some(prev) = ctx.counters.get(&ck) { ... }`, so its DashMap guard is already dropped before line 416.

Line 416 is `drop(ctx.counters.get(&ck));` — it acquires a fresh read guard and immediately drops it, changing nothing; the following `insert` at 417 works either way because `get` returns a shared guard.
The statement reads as if it were releasing the lock taken at 408, so a reviewer looking for the lock discipline in this hot path is sent down a false trail.

issues.summary: triage-agent's Deps carries an unused OpensearchClient behind allow(dead_code) and still fails boot when OPENSEARCH_URL is unset
issues.suggestion: Drop the `os` field, its `#[allow(dead_code)]` and the `.context("OPENSEARCH_URL not set")?` construction; keep only `os_url` (already defaulted to localhost:9200 at 363-366) so triage no longer requires an OpenSearch URL it does not use.
evidence: crates/triage-agent/src/main.rs:246-249: `/// Kept for parity with the connector config; verdict writes go through `http` because `OpensearchClient` exposes search only.` followed by `#[allow(dead_code)] os: Arc<OpensearchClient>`.

The field's own comment explains why it is not needed (the verdict write goes through `os_url` + raw HTTP at 140-163), which is a doc comment doing the job of a deletion.

issues.summary: enrich_cve hand-rolls the Redis get/set logic in four nested if-lets while cache_get/cache_set sit unused ten lines above
issues.suggestion: Extend the existing helpers instead of bypassing them: add a `cache_get_raw(&self, key) -> Option<String>` (returning the stored `"null"` sentinel as-is) and a `cache_set_with_ttl(&self, key, payload, ttl)`; enrich_cve then becomes three flat lines per branch and keeps cache_set's warn-on-failure behaviour.

crates/enrichment-lib/src/lib.rs:434-446 then re-implements the read path inline: `if let Some(client) = &self.redis { if let Ok(mut conn) = ... { if let Ok(Some(raw)) = ... { if raw == "null" ...` — four nesting levels to express one cache lookup with a negative-cache sentinel.

Lines 449-464 repeat the same three-level nesting twice more for the positive and negative write paths, and the write errors are discarded with `let _: redis::RedisResult<()>`, unlike `cache_set` which warns.
Two cache access styles in one impl means the next person adding a cached call has to choose which to copy.

issues.summary: NvdClient::list_published duplicates the query assembly that list_modified reaches through the shared list_window helper
issues.suggestion: Make `list_published` call `self.list_window("pubStartDate", "pubEndDate", from, to, start_index, extra)` and delete its inline body, leaving one place that knows the query parameter names.

issues.summary: idem_key round-trips a String through serde_json, and failure ToolResults are hand-built in four places despite a ToolResult::retryable constructor
issues.suggestion: Replace idem_key's body with `(!call.idempotency_key.is_empty()).then(|| call.idempotency_key.clone())`, and add one `ToolResult::failed(call_id, error)` constructor next to `retryable` so all six failure sites in main.rs use a named shape.
evidence: crates/tool-server/src/main.rs:45-49: `serde_json::to_value(&call.idempotency_key).ok().and_then(|v| v.as_str().filter(|s| !s.is_empty()).map(str::to_string))` — `idempotency_key` is already a `String` (crates/agent-protocol/src/tool.rs:22), so the value→JSON→&str→String round trip exists only to test emptiness.

The same file builds `ToolResult { call_id, ok: false, output: Value::Null, error: Some(...) }` by hand at lines 91-100, 104-113, 136-141 and 158-166, while `ToolResult::retryable` (crates/agent-protocol/src/tool.rs:83-93) is used for the two idempotency paths at 143-153.
Two construction styles for one type inside one 40-line region make it unclear whether the `output: Null` failures are meaningfully different from the `retryable` ones.

issues.summary: POST /invoke is implemented three times with divergent verdict handling; agent-core's ToolGateway is never used
issues.suggestion: Move the {decision, result} envelope and one invoke(call) -> InvokeOutcome helper into agent-protocol (or agent-core) and have response-agent and detection-agent call it; model transport failure as its own outcome variant instead of fabricating a Deny verdict, and promote the retryable flag to a real field on ToolResult.
evidence: crates/agent-core/src/gateway.rs:36-39 declares ToolGateway with retry- and idempotency-aware invoke, but no crate outside agent-core ever constructs HttpToolGateway, even though response-agent and triage-agent already depend on agent-core.

crates/response-agent/src/main.rs:210-232 re-implements the call as invoke_tool with no retry, and synthesizes DecisionKind::Deny when the transport fails (lines 212-224), so an unreachable tool server is stored in response_actions as a policy denial and emitted as 'denied by policy' (line 290, 327-332).

crates/detection-agent/src/pipeline.rs:263-270 treats any HTTP 2xx as success and never reads the decision field, so a policy denial - which tool-server returns as HTTP 200 with a deny verdict per crates/tool-server/src/main.rs:5-6 - is logged as 'detection.sigma.deploy audited'.

The {decision, result} wire struct is declared three times: crates/tool-server/src/main.rs:29-33, crates/agent-core/src/gateway.rs:28-32, crates/response-agent/src/main.rs:189-195, so a shape change requires three coordinated edits with no compiler help.
The retry hint travels out of band inside ToolResult.output under a magic key (crates/agent-protocol/src/tool.rs:65-79), which only the unused gateway reads.

issues.summary: ActivityEvent is declared four times plus one hand-rolled producer, and its subject constant five times
issues.suggestion: Define ActivityEvent and SUBJECT_ACTIVITY once in agent-protocol next to the other subjects, delete the four module copies, and make vuln-agent construct the type so an omitted correlation id becomes a compile error.
evidence: Four near-identical copies of ActivityEvent live in crates/triage-agent/src/activity.rs, crates/response-agent/src/activity.rs, crates/hunt-agent/src/activity.rs and crates/detection-agent/src/activity.rs; they have already drifted - triage's step is &'static str (triage-agent/src/activity.rs:22) while the other three use String (response-agent/src/activity.rs:20).

issues.summary: Envelope publish is re-implemented in six services, so message durability depends on which service produced it
issues.suggestion: Add publish(subject, &Envelope) (JetStream-first with fallback) to agent-protocol beside the Envelope type, then delete NatsBus, a2a::publish, bas-runner's publish and the inline publishes in favour of it.
evidence: crates/ingestion-gateway/src/nats_sink.rs:71-91 implements the JetStream-first publish with plain fallback; crates/api-server/src/a2a.rs:235-276 duplicates the stream creation and the same publish policy, with a comment admitting 'same policy as ingestion-gateway's NatsSink'.

Each copy repeats the same serialize/publish/warn shape, so a change to subject policy or logging has to be applied in six places.

issues.summary: Triage passes the case id to response only inside a thehive:// URI; the receiver defaults the id to "unknown"
issues.suggestion: Add a typed case identifier (or a CaseRef struct) to HandoffPayload/Artifact so the id crosses the boundary as data; keep ref_uri purely for retrieval.
evidence: Producer: crates/triage-agent/src/main.rs:218-223 carries the case id only as ref_uri: format!("thehive://case/{case_id}") with kind: "case"; no field on Artifact or HandoffPayload holds an identifier.

Consumer: crates/response-agent/src/main.rs:175-186 recovers it with find(|a| a.kind == "case").strip_prefix("thehive://case/")...unwrap_or_else(|| "unknown"), so any producer that changes the URI scheme silently degrades to the literal "unknown".
That literal then becomes response_actions.case_id (response-agent/src/main.rs:319) and the TheHive case patched at line 347, so a mismatch writes plan data under a case that does not exist.

issues.summary: The orchestrator subscribes to ares.* which includes its own DLQ subject, so unparseable messages republish forever
issues.suggestion: Subscribe to the concrete routed subjects instead of ares.*, or exclude the dlq/activity subjects explicitly, and move the DLQ outside the subscribed namespace (e.g. ares.dlq.>) with a hop counter so a redelivered poison message terminates.
evidence: crates/orchestrator/src/main.rs:133 subscribes to "ares.*", and SUBJECT_DLQ is "ares.dlq" (main.rs:35), which the wildcard matches.

On a parse failure main.rs:79-83 publishes the raw payload to SUBJECT_DLQ; the orchestrator receives its own publish, delivery_count() returns 1 when no Nats-Delivery-Count header is present (main.rs:120-128), the payload still fails to parse, and it is published again - an unbounded loop with no delay.

ares.activity messages are ActivityEvent JSON, never Envelope JSON, so every activity event in the pipeline takes that path (producers: crates/triage-agent/src/main.rs:79-91 and the other four agents).

issues.summary: EvalCtx.asset_classes is never populated, so the protected host-class rule is dead; the &mut signature also forces a global mutex
issues.suggestion: Populate asset classes where the policy set is loaded (PolicyEngine::load) or accept them on the engine, change evaluate to take &EvalCtx, and drop the tool-server mutex so tool calls stop serializing on a read-only map.

The only construction site in the workspace is crates/tool-server/src/main.rs:239 EvalCtx::new(), which leaves the map empty; nothing ever inserts into it, so a host with a protected class is allowed through.

lib.rs:314 takes ctx: &mut EvalCtx, which forces crates/tool-server/src/main.rs:41 to hold a Mutex<EvalCtx> and lock it around every /invoke (main.rs:66-69), although all mutation goes through the Arc<DashMap> counters (lib.rs:47) and asset_classes is read-only.

issues.summary: Kill-switch state is read by two implementations whose file semantics disagree
issues.suggestion: Move the single kill-switch read into agent-protocol (both crates already depend on it) and delete the policy-engine copy so the two layers cannot disagree.
evidence: crates/agent-core/src/kill.rs:31-35 reports engaged when the path is a file with len > 0, so a whitespace-only kill file engages the switch.
crates/policy-engine/src/lib.rs:426-439 re-implements the same check and reports engaged only when read_to_string(...).trim() is non-empty, so the same file disengages the policy engine.

crates/api-server/src/kill.rs:34-52 is the writer for that file and reports the state through agent_core::kill_switch_engaged(), so the console can show 'engaged' while tool-server evaluates calls as allowed.
policy-engine cannot depend on agent-core (no such dependency in crates/policy-engine/Cargo.toml), which is why the logic was copied instead of shared.

issues.summary: Connector clients expose only some verbs, so three callers hand-roll HTTP with their own credential reads
issues.suggestion: Add index_doc to OpensearchClient and query to ThehiveClient (returning Value) and route the three call sites through them, so auth, retry and error mapping stay in one place.
evidence: OpensearchClient exposes only query (crates/connectors/src/lib.rs:147-157), so crates/triage-agent/src/main.rs:146-157 and crates/detection-agent/src/pipeline.rs:234-241 each POST raw with their own OPENSEARCH_URL/USER/PASS reads.
ThehiveClient has no query method (connectors/src/lib.rs:230-276), so crates/api-server/src/main.rs:139-152 rebuilds the client inline from THEHIVE_URL and THEHIVE_API_KEY.
These paths bypass the shared auth and retry helper (send_with_retry, connectors/src/lib.rs:79-123), so the documented 15s resilience contract holds only for calls that go through the connector.
Both modules document the gap in comments instead of closing it, so the workaround is now the established pattern.

issues.summary: DecisionKind to string is hand-written in tool-server and re-typed as SQL literals in two other crates
issues.suggestion: Serialize DecisionKind with serde instead of a hand-written label, and document the stored column as the serde value so the three sites agree by construction.
evidence: crates/tool-server/src/main.rs:52-58 hand-maps DecisionKind to "allow"/"deny"/"approval_required" even though crates/agent-protocol/src/tool.rs:30-32 already serializes exactly those labels via rename_all = "snake_case".

crates/bas-runner/src/main.rs:154-156 matches the stored text with WHERE decision = 'allow', and crates/api-server/src/main.rs:186-192 returns the same column to the console, so the vocabulary is fixed in three unrelated places.
Adding a DecisionKind variant compiles everywhere while the SQL literals silently stop matching.

issues.summary: The policy->audit->idempotency->execute composition in tool-server /invoke has no test
issues.suggestion: Add a #[cfg(test)] module in crates/tool-server/src/main.rs that builds `AppState` with the real PolicyEngine over `../../policies`, a `Store::mem()` and `audit: None`, then calls `invoke` through `Router::oneshot` with three calls: an allowlisted tool (assert decision allow + result.ok), `host.shutdown` (assert deny + result.error starts with 'denied:' + no executor invoked), and the same idempotency key twice (assert second response replays the first result).
evidence: crates/tool-server/src/main.rs:60 `invoke` is the only path to side effects in the system; the file contains no #[cfg(test)] module.
`execute` (line 109) and `run_tool` (line 151) decide whether a denied call can still reach an executor and whether an idempotency replay returns the stored result; both are unexercised.

The two halves are tested separately (policy-engine 11 tests, idempotency 9 tests), so nothing verifies the contract that a Deny decision never calls `run_tool`, or that an audit-writer failure degrades to a log line instead of failing the request.
The only tool-server test touching the registry is executors/mod.rs:800 `registry_covers_policy_tools`, which asserts allowlist/executor name parity, not behaviour.

issues.summary: All agent binaries (triage, response, detection, hunt, vuln) have zero tests for their decision logic
issues.suggestion: Extract the per-alert decision into a testable function and cover it: in triage-agent add `#[cfg(test)]` tests for `severity_gte_high` (high/critical vs medium) and `typed_iocs` type mapping; in response-agent add a table test asserting `rollback_for` returns the inverse tool for all 8 reversible tools and `None` for read-only ones. Both are single-file additions in main.rs following the existing inline-module convention.

Pure helpers in the same file are untested and trivially testable: `severity_gte_high` (line 66) and `typed_iocs` (line 94).

crates/response-agent/src/main.rs:104 `rollback_for` maps each side-effecting tool to its inverse (blocklist.ip.remove, wazuh unisolate_host, ad.user.enable, ...) and `case_id_of` (line 175) parses the handoff; both untested, so a wrong rollback mapping would ship silently into the `response_actions` table.

The codebase already has the seams for this (`MockProvider` in llm-client, `ToolGateway`/`CheckpointStore` traits used by agent-core tests), so the gap is not technical impossibility.

issues.summary: connectors (1,189 LOC, 6 HTTP clients) tests only JSON parsing; retry, budget and throttle logic is unverified
issues.suggestion: Make `retry_sleep` and the throttle delay computation pure and assert them (`retry_sleep(0, 1s) == 250ms`, capped by `remaining`, exponential growth), and route the clients' HTTP call through a small `HttpTransport` trait implemented by reqwest in prod and by a scripted fake in tests so `call` can be tested for 429-then-success and deadline-exceeded cases.
evidence: The 3 tests at crates/connectors/src/lib.rs:1141-1188 cover MISP attribute deserialization and warning-list matching only.

`retry_sleep` (line 67) and the `call` retry loop with `CALL_BUDGET` (lines 84-120) implement backoff and deadline handling; a regression here means either hammering a SOAR API or timing out silently, and nothing asserts the schedule or the give-up path.
Per-client throttling at line 913 (`sleep(self.min_interval - elapsed)`) and the 1<<attempt backoff at line 950 are untested.

The clients are concrete structs (OpensearchClient:130, ThehiveClient:214, CortexClient:277, MispClient:429, WazuhClient:562, NvdClient:885) with no trait seam, which is also why triage/response/detection `process()` cannot be tested without network access.

issues.summary: detection-agent pipeline has zero tests for Sigma validation, Lucene conversion and rule promotion
issues.suggestion: Add `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in pipeline.rs covering: `validate_sigma` rejects YAML missing `detection`/`logsource` and accepts a minimal valid rule; `naive_lucene` maps a two-key selection to 'a:1 AND b:2' and errors on a non-scalar-only selection; `slugify("LSASS Access! (v2)") == "lsass-access-v2"`; `write_pending` + `promote_and_commit` run against a tempdir (parameterize the two dir consts).

`write_pending` (line 91) writes agent-generated YAML into detection-content/pending and `promote_and_commit` (line 170) renames into detection-content/active and shells out to `git add`/`git commit` — the detection-as-code promotion path, entirely unverified.
`validate_sigma`'s fallback branch (no `sigma` binary on PATH) is the branch CI actually exercises, and it is untested.
Agent output is LLM-authored, so validation is the only guard between a malformed draft and an active rule.

issues.summary: orchestrator dedupe key/day-bucket logic is untested; a wrong key silently drops or duplicates alerts
issues.suggestion: Add tests in dedupe.rs: same envelope yields a stable 64-char hex key; changing only `ts` within the same day keeps the key; crossing midnight changes it; missing `rule.id` or `agent.name` still produces a deterministic key (assert equality across two calls rather than the exact hash).
evidence: `dedupe_key` (crates/orchestrator/src/dedupe.rs:49) hashes source + rule.id + host + 24h bucket; `day_bucket` (line 77) renders YYYY-MM-DD. Neither has a test and the file has no #[cfg(test)] module.
The key falls back to `envelope.payload['host']` when `agent.name` is absent (lines 61-67) and to an empty string when `rule.id` is missing — both silent-degradation branches with no assertion.
A key collision suppresses a real alert (dedupe returns true); a key split duplicates work. Both failure modes are invisible in the current suite.

issues.summary: api-server A2A/ACP endpoints and input validators have no behavioural tests; only router construction is asserted
issues.suggestion: Add one axum-level test module in api-server (using `api_router().oneshot(...)` as http-limits already does) asserting: unknown agent name -> 404 on `/a2a/agents/{name}`, `POST /a2a/triage-agent` with a malformed JSON-RPC body -> INVALID_PARAMS, and `/vulns/not-a-cve` -> 400. Then unit-test `valid_cve_id` against 'CVE-2024-1234' (true), 'CVE-24-1234' (false), 'cve-2024-1234' (false).
evidence: crates/api-server/src/a2a.rs (640 LOC) and crates/api-server/src/acp.rs (634 LOC) contain no tests; the single api-server test (main.rs:387) only calls `api_router()` to prove route path syntax compiles.
Pure, deterministic helpers are untested: `card_for` (a2a.rs:145), `orchestrator_card` (a2a.rs:176), `manifest_for` (acp.rs:60), `input_to_text` (acp.rs:221), `run_event` (acp.rs:487).

`valid_cve_id` (vulns.rs:18) is a hand-rolled byte-index validator (len >= 13, `id[8] == '-'`, all digits after 9) guarding outbound NVD calls; it has no test, and neither does the `days` clamp in `list_vulns` (vulns.rs:52).
JSON-RPC dispatch itself is well covered in a2a/src/rpc.rs (5 tests), so the missing coverage is the HTTP/axum layer that wraps it.

issues.summary: The 19-row documented policy denial matrix has ~9 rows with no assertion in the policy-engine tests
issues.suggestion: Add one `#[tokio::test]` per missing matrix row in policy-engine's test module (each is 5 lines: build a ToolCall, evaluate, assert DecisionKind::Deny and a reason substring), or better, drive the table from evals/policy_tests.md by parsing it in a test so the spec and the suite cannot drift.
evidence: evals/policy_tests.md rows 8 (protected CIDR via `firewall.rule.add`), 9 (enum violation), 15 (control-plane `self.services`), 16 (missing required arg on `kill_process`), 17 (`rule_path` pattern), 18 (CVE-id pattern) and 19 (CVSS vector pattern) have no corresponding test in crates/policy-engine/src/lib.rs:536-723.

`firewall.rule.add`, `nvd.lookup_cve`, `cvss.score`, `detection.sigma.deploy` and `wazuh.active_response.kill_process` never appear in any test assertion — only in executors and the bas-runner allowlist.
Protected-user patterns from policies/protected-assets.yml ("Administrator", "krbtgt", "^svc-siem$", "root$") are untested; `protected_user_is_denied` only asserts "svc-agent".
Rows that are covered (1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 14, approval, kill switch) show the pattern is established, so the gap is mechanical rather than conceptual.

issues.summary: No cross-module or end-to-end tests exist; the eval harness is a documented TODO
issues.suggestion: Add `crates/api-server/tests/` (or a new `crates/integration-tests` member) with two or three tests that spin the axum routers in-process against in-memory fakes (no NATS/Postgres), asserting the full request->policy->response shape for one allow and one deny. In parallel, implement the `evals/run.sh` TODO for the existing triage_seed.jsonl using MockProvider so precision/recall becomes a CI signal.
evidence: No `crates/*/tests/` directory exists in the workspace; `cargo test --workspace` therefore only runs inline unit tests.

The seams that carry real risk — NATS subjects between orchestrator/agents, Postgres `response_actions` and `seen_alerts`, tool-server HTTP contract `{decision, result}` — are never exercised together by any test.
